origin_region: Hsinchu · Emei and Beipu; Miaoli · Toufen and Sanwan
cultivar: Qingxin Damou (Qing Xin Da Mou) in Hsinchu and Miaoli; Qingxin oolong for the lighter 'white-tip' versions from Pinglin and Shiding
processing: Hand-picked bud-and-two-leaf shoots bitten by the tea green leafhopper, withered and oxidised to roughly 60–75%, pan-fired, then wrapped in damp cloth to rest and soften before rolling (the hui ruan step) and dried at low heat; no roast, and no pesticides because the insects are needed.
harvest_season: One main harvest in early summer, around the Grain in Ear solar term in June, when leafhopper activity peaks; small autumn pickings exist but the June tea is what the name means.
appearance_dry: Loose, twisted leaves in five colours, white fuzzy buds with green, yellow, red and brown leaf, soft and light in the hand.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber-orange, like a light honey.
appearance_wet: Small, soft leaves with brown-red edges and pale buds, bitten and puckered at the margins.
taste_profile: Honey, ripe peach and muscat grape with a silky, almost fizzy sweetness and no astringency; cooler brewing keeps it soft.

brewing.notes: Cooler than other oolongs, around 85 °C, with the gaiwan filled generously because the leaf is light and bulky; boiling water flattens it and brings out sourness. Also Western-style at 3 g per cup, and a superb cold brew.

vintage_note: Sold by summer harvest year and above all by competition grade: the Hsinchu County farmers' associations (Emei, Beipu) grade lots from Special through First, Second and Third and sell them in sealed packs, often of just 75 g, at prices that climb steeply with the grade and the share of white buds. Garden tea is sold as the June harvest of the current year; it keeps two or three years sealed and is not usually aged. Lighter 'white-tip oolong' from Pinglin and Shiding is a cheaper cousin made from Qing Xin oolong.
description:
Oriental Beauty is the heavily oxidised, white-tipped oolong of the Hakka hill country of Hsinchu and Miaoli, and the tea that made leafhopper damage a virtue. The tea green leafhopper feeds on the young shoots in early summer, the bush responds by producing the compounds that smell of honey and ripe fruit, and the farmers of Emei, Beipu, Toufen and Sanwan turn that damaged leaf into one of the most expensive teas in Taiwan. Locals call it Peng Feng Cha, 'braggart's tea', after the story of the farmer nobody believed when he said how much he had sold it for; the English name is said to come from a European royal, which is a legend.

It is picked once a year in the way that matters, around the Grain in Ear solar term in June, by hand, as a bud and two leaves from unsprayed gardens of the Qing Xin Da Mou cultivar. The leaf is withered and oxidised to roughly 60 to 75 percent, pan-fired, then wrapped in damp cloth to rest and soften before being rolled and dried at low heat. There is no roast. The finished leaf shows five colours, white buds and green, yellow, red and brown leaf, which is where the name 'five-colour tea' comes from.

The cup is honey, ripe peach and muscat grape with a silky, almost fizzy sweetness and no astringency at all. Brew it cooler than other oolongs, around 85 degrees, with the gaiwan filled generously because the leaf is light and bulky; boiling water flattens it and brings out a sourness. It gives five or six steeps gongfu-style, works Western-style at three grams per cup, and cold-brews into something close to a dessert wine.

It is sold by summer harvest year and, above all, by competition grade: the Hsinchu County farmers' associations grade lots from Special through First, Second and Third and sell them in sealed packs, often of just 75 grams, at prices that climb steeply with the grade and the proportion of white buds. The lighter 'white-tip oolong' of Pinglin and Shiding is made from Qing Xin oolong and is a cheaper cousin, and a lot of 'Oriental Beauty' from Thailand, Vietnam and mainland China is sold without saying so. Honey in the empty cup and bitten, puckered leaf edges are the tell.

It keeps two or three years sealed and is not usually aged. Serve it with pastry or after a meal; it is the oolong to convert people who think they only like black tea.
sources_note: Competition grade names follow the general Taiwanese farmers' association scheme; the exact tier list for the Emei and Beipu competitions should be checked. The 'named by a European queen' story is flagged as legend.
